title: Virtualization and cloud basics
summary: Understand what virtual machines are and why technicians use them, run a VM with Hyper-V, and learn the core cloud service and deployment models you will meet on the helpdesk.
objectives: Explain what a hypervisor and a virtual machine are
Create and manage a Hyper-V virtual machine from PowerShell
Describe the cloud service models: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS
Tell public, private and hybrid cloud deployment models apart
Recognise common support scenarios involving VMs and cloud apps

Software that creates and runs virtual machines
quiz.why: A hypervisor is the software layer that creates, runs and manages virtual machines by sharing the physical hardware among them.
Type 1 hypervisors such as Hyper-V or ESXi run directly on the hardware, while type 2 hypervisors like VirtualBox run as an application on top of an existing operating system.

quiz.q: A company uses Microsoft 365 — email and Office in the browser with nothing to install or patch on the server side. Which cloud model is that?
quiz.why: Software as a Service delivers ready-to-use applications over the internet, with the provider managing everything underneath; the customer just uses the app.

quiz.q: Which PowerShell command lists the virtual machines on a Hyper-V host?
quiz.why: Get-VM returns the virtual machines and their state on a Hyper-V host; the others list processes, services, or files.

quiz.q: In one sentence, explain the difference between IaaS and PaaS.
quiz.answer: IaaS gives you raw virtual machines, storage and networking that you manage yourself, while PaaS gives you a managed platform to run your code without managing the underlying servers.
quiz.why: IaaS hands you the infrastructure (you patch the OS); PaaS abstracts the servers away so you only deal with your application, trading control for convenience.

quiz.q: Why might an organisation choose a hybrid cloud over a purely public cloud?
quiz.answer: To keep sensitive or regulated data and some workloads on their own private infrastructure while still using public cloud for scale, bursting, or cheaper general workloads.
quiz.why: Hybrid combines private control for sensitive systems with public-cloud flexibility and scale, which is why regulated industries often adopt it.

body_markdown:
## What virtualization actually means

**Virtualization** lets one physical computer pretend to be many. A **virtual machine (VM)** is a complete computer — its own OS, disk, and network — running as software inside another machine. The thing that makes this possible is the **hypervisor**, the software layer that shares the real hardware (CPU, RAM, disk) among several VMs and keeps them isolated from each other.

For a helpdesk technician this is everyday gold: you can test a risky fix, run an old application, or reproduce a user's problem on a throwaway VM without touching a production machine.

## Type 1 vs type 2 hypervisors

There are two kinds. A **type 1 (bare-metal)** hypervisor runs directly on the hardware with no host OS underneath — think **Hyper-V** on a server or VMware **ESXi**. A **type 2 (hosted)** hypervisor runs as an application on top of your existing OS — think **VirtualBox** or VMware Workstation on your laptop. Type 1 is for servers and performance; type 2 is for convenience on a desktop.

## Running a VM with Hyper-V

Windows includes **Hyper-V** (a type 1 hypervisor) on Pro and Enterprise editions. Manage it with PowerShell:

```powershell
# See what VMs exist and their state
Get-VM

# Create a new VM with 4 GB RAM and a new virtual disk
New-VM -Name "Test-Win11" -MemoryStartupBytes 4GB -NewVHDPath "C:\VMs\test.vhdx" -NewVHDSizeBytes 60GB

# Start it
Start-VM -Name "Test-Win11"
```

Sample output:

```powershell
Name        State   CPUUsage(%)   MemoryAssigned(M)   Uptime
----        -----   -----------   -----------------   ------
Test-Win11  Running 1             4096                00:00:42
```

## The cloud: someone else's computer, on demand

The **cloud** is computing you rent over the internet instead of owning. The three classic **service models** describe how much the provider manages for you:

- **IaaS** (Infrastructure as a Service): you rent raw VMs, storage and networking, and you manage the OS and apps. Example: an Azure or AWS virtual machine.
- **PaaS** (Platform as a Service): you deploy your code onto a managed platform and never touch the servers.
- **SaaS** (Software as a Service): you just use a finished app in the browser. Example: Microsoft 365 or Gmail.

A quick way to spin up cloud infrastructure with the Azure CLI:

```bash
# Log in, then create a resource group and a small VM
az login
az group create --name demo-rg --location uksouth
az vm create --resource-group demo-rg --name demo-vm --image Ubuntu2204 --size Standard_B1s
```

## Deployment models

Where the cloud lives matters too. **Public cloud** is shared infrastructure run by a provider (Azure, AWS). **Private cloud** is dedicated infrastructure for one organisation. **Hybrid cloud** mixes both — keeping sensitive data private while using public cloud for scale. Regulated industries often choose hybrid for exactly this reason.

## Your task

If you have Windows Pro/Enterprise, enable Hyper-V, then use `Get-VM` to list any existing VMs and `New-VM` to create one (you can delete it afterwards with `Remove-VM`). If Hyper-V is not available, install VirtualBox and create a small Linux VM instead. Then write a short note classifying three real services you use — for example a hosted email service, a rented server, and a code-hosting platform — into IaaS, PaaS or SaaS, and explain your reasoning for each.

slides.narration: Welcome to lesson eight. Virtual machines and the cloud are everywhere on a modern helpdesk, and you'll be expected to understand both. In this lesson we'll cover what a hypervisor and a virtual machine are, how to run one with Hyper-V, and the core cloud models: I-a-a-S, P-a-a-S, and S-a-a-S. By the end you'll be able to spin up a test V M and classify cloud services with confidence.

slides.title: The cloud, in one line
bullets: Computing you rent over the internet.
You don't own the hardware.
Pay for what you use, scale on demand.
Service models describe who manages what.
slides.narration: Now the cloud. In one line, it's computing you rent over the internet instead of owning. You don't buy the hardware; you pay for what you use and scale up or down on demand. The key idea to learn is the service models, which simply describe how much the provider manages for you versus how much you manage yourself. There are three you must know.

slides.title: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
bullets: IaaS: rent raw VMs, you manage the OS.
PaaS: deploy code, provider runs the servers.
SaaS: just use a finished app in the browser.
More managed = less control, more convenience.
slides.narration: Three service models. Infrastructure as a service, I-a-a-S, rents you raw virtual machines, storage, and networking, and you manage the operating system and apps. Platform as a service, P-a-a-S, gives you a managed platform to run your code without touching servers. Software as a service, S-a-a-S, is a finished app in the browser, like Microsoft three sixty-five. The more the provider manages, the less control but the more convenience you get.

slides.title: Spinning up cloud with the CLI
bullets: az login authenticates you.
Create a resource group to hold things.
az vm create makes a virtual machine.
The same idea exists in the AWS CLI.
slides.code:
az login
az group create --name demo-rg --location uksouth
az vm create --resource-group demo-rg --name demo-vm --image Ubuntu2204 --size Standard_B1s
slides.narration: You can create cloud infrastructure from the command line. With the Azure C-L-I, you run a-z login to authenticate, a-z group create to make a resource group that holds your resources, and a-z v-m create to spin up a virtual machine, choosing an image and a size. The A-W-S command-line tool works the same way with different command names. This is I-a-a-S in action.

slides.title: Deployment models
bullets: Public: shared infrastructure from a provider.
Private: dedicated to one organisation.
Hybrid: a mix of public and private.
Hybrid keeps sensitive data private.
slides.narration: Where the cloud lives matters too. Public cloud is shared infrastructure run by a provider like Azure or A-W-S. Private cloud is dedicated infrastructure for a single organisation. Hybrid cloud mixes both, keeping sensitive or regulated data on private infrastructure while using public cloud for scale. Regulated industries, like banking and healthcare, often choose hybrid for exactly that reason.

slides.title: Why this matters on the helpdesk
bullets: Reproduce user problems on a VM safely.
Many apps users 'install' are really SaaS.
Cloud outages and logins become support calls.
Knowing the model speeds up troubleshooting.
slides.narration: Why does this matter day to day? You'll reproduce user problems on a throwaway V M without risking production. Many of the apps users think they installed are really software as a service, so the fix lives in a browser or a provider's dashboard. Cloud logins and outages turn into support calls. Knowing which model you're dealing with tells you where the problem, and the fix, actually live.
